title: 02 — Features and Feature Stores
html:
02 — Features and Feature Stores

The one idea: a feature is only valid if it could have been known at the moment the prediction is made. Build every training row with a point-in-time join, compute features once in a governed place, and serve exactly the same values online as you trained on.

1. What it is

  • Feature engineering: turning raw data into model inputs. For example ratios (debt / EBITDA), changes (rating notches moved in 12 months), aggregates (average monthly flow over 3 months), and encodings of categories.
  • Point-in-time (as-of) join: for each label date, take the latest feature value known at or before that date.
  • Feature store: a governed catalogue of feature tables with keys, timestamps, lineage and owners. It gives one definition for training and serving.
  • Training-serving skew: the model sees different values (or differently computed values) in production than in training.

2. Why it matters

  • The bitemporal tables of a financial data platform record both when a fact was true and when it was known. That is exactly what point-in-time joins need. Use knowledge time, not valid time, so restated figures don't leak into the past.
  • Shared features stop duplication. Every team computing "leverage" differently is a governance and accuracy problem.
  • Online inference (an API scoring an issuer now) needs low-latency lookups of the same features.

3. The main ideas, beginner to expert

3.1 Beginner: good features

Kind Example Watch out for
Ratio Interest coverage = EBIT / interest Division by zero, negative denominators
Change Notches downgraded in 12 months Needs history at the right knowledge time
Window aggregate 3-month average net flow Window must end before the label date
Category Sector, SEBI scheme category Rare categories: group them, or use target encoding fitted on train only
Text-derived Sentiment of a rating rationale Model version must be recorded

3.2 Intermediate: point-in-time correctness

---
title: Point-in-time join — only values known before the label date
---
flowchart LR
    F1["leverage 2.8<br/>known 2026-01-10"] --> L1["label row<br/>as of 2026-03-31"]
    F2["leverage 3.9<br/>known 2026-04-12"] --> L2["label row<br/>as of 2026-06-30"]
    F3["leverage 5.1<br/>known 2026-07-15"] -. "not allowed for either row" .-> L1

Use knowledge time (when the platform learned the value). If an annual report for March was published in June, a March 31 label row must not see it.

3.3 Senior: feature stores on Databricks (checked 2026-10-26)

  • Feature tables in Unity Catalog are Delta tables with a primary key, plus an optional timestamp key for point-in-time lookups. Unity Catalog provides governance, lineage, point-in-time joins and sharing.
  • Feature Views are the newer, recommended way to declare features, with time-windowed aggregations. They are in Public Preview.
  • Online Feature Stores are backed by Lakebase (autoscaling Postgres), synced from offline tables in one of three modes: TRIGGERED (the default), CONTINUOUS or SNAPSHOT.
  • Model Serving can look up features automatically at request time, and Feature Serving endpoints serve features to outside applications.
  • Workspaces created before 19 August 2024 without Unity Catalog may still have the legacy Workspace Feature Store.
# Not run: requires Databricks with the feature engineering client. Names are made up.
from databricks.feature_engineering import FeatureEngineeringClient, FeatureLookup
fe = FeatureEngineeringClient()
fe.create_table(name="fin.features.issuer_credit", primary_keys=["issuer_id", "known_at"],
                timeseries_columns="known_at", df=issuer_features_df)
training_set = fe.create_training_set(
    df=labels_df,                                   # issuer_id, as_of, label
    feature_lookups=[FeatureLookup(table_name="fin.features.issuer_credit",
                                   lookup_key="issuer_id", timestamp_lookup_key="as_of")],
    label="downgraded_next_90d")
train_df = training_set.load_df()                   # point-in-time correct join

The parameter names (timeseries_columns, timestamp_lookup_key) follow the documented client API, but check the current reference for your version, because the authoring options changed with Feature Views.

4. Working code

The script builds training rows two ways, a naive "latest value" join and a point-in-time join, then checks served values against offline values for skew. pandas only.

import pandas as pd

# Point-in-time correctness: a training row may only use features that were KNOWN at its label time.
# Feature values with the time we learned them (knowledge time), for two made-up issuers.
features = pd.DataFrame({
    "issuer":   ["A", "A", "A", "B", "B"],
    "known_at": pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-10", "2026-04-12", "2026-07-15", "2026-02-01", "2026-06-20"]),
    "leverage": [2.8, 3.9, 5.1, 2.1, 2.3],
})
# Training labels: on each date, did the issuer get downgraded in the next 90 days?
labels = pd.DataFrame({
    "issuer":   ["A", "A", "B"],
    "as_of":    pd.to_datetime(["2026-03-31", "2026-06-30", "2026-03-31"]),
    "downgraded_next_90d": [0, 1, 0],
})

# WRONG: join on the latest feature value. Every row sees July's leverage, including the March row.
latest = features.sort_values("known_at").groupby("issuer").tail(1)
wrong = labels.merge(latest[["issuer", "leverage"]], on="issuer")
print("Naive join (leaks the future):")
print(wrong.to_string(index=False))

# RIGHT: an as-of join takes the last value known at or before each label date.
right = pd.merge_asof(labels.sort_values("as_of"), features.sort_values("known_at"),
                      left_on="as_of", right_on="known_at", by="issuer", direction="backward")
print("\nPoint-in-time join:")
print(right[["issuer", "as_of", "known_at", "leverage", "downgraded_next_90d"]].to_string(index=False))

# Training/serving skew check: the online value must equal the offline value for the same key and time.
offline = right.set_index(["issuer", "as_of"])["leverage"]
online_served = {("A", pd.Timestamp("2026-06-30")): 3.9, ("A", pd.Timestamp("2026-03-31")): 3.9}
for key, served in online_served.items():
    status = "ok" if offline[key] == served else f"SKEW (offline {offline[key]})"
    print(f"served {key[0]} {key[1].date()} leverage={served}: {status}")

Output:

Naive join (leaks the future):
issuer      as_of  downgraded_next_90d  leverage
     A 2026-03-31                    0       5.1
     A 2026-06-30                    1       5.1
     B 2026-03-31                    0       2.3

Point-in-time join:
issuer      as_of   known_at  leverage  downgraded_next_90d
     A 2026-03-31 2026-01-10       2.8                    0
     B 2026-03-31 2026-02-01       2.1                    0
     A 2026-06-30 2026-04-12       3.9                    1
served A 2026-06-30 leverage=3.9: ok
served A 2026-03-31 leverage=3.9: SKEW (offline 2.8)

What to notice:

  • The naive join gives the March row a leverage of 5.1, a value learned in July. The model would learn from the future, and validation would look great.
  • merge_asof with direction="backward" gives each row the last value known at or before its date. The March row gets 2.8.
  • The second served value doesn't match the offline value for the same key and time. That is training-serving skew, and catching it needs a logged comparison like this one.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Joining on valid time instead of knowledge time. Restatements leak backwards.
  2. Window aggregates that include the label date. End every window strictly before the prediction time.
  3. Computing features differently in training and serving code. Use one definition, from the feature store.
  4. Target encoding on all data. Fit it on training folds only.
  5. No timestamp key on feature tables. Point-in-time lookups become impossible.

6. Exercise (1.5 hours)

  1. Add a feature "change in leverage over the previous known value" and build it point-in-time correctly.
  2. Add a second feature table (rating outlook) and join both as-of the label date.
  3. Write a check that fails if any training row has known_at > as_of.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What makes a feature point-in-time correct?
  2. Why use knowledge time rather than valid time for training joins?
  3. What is training-serving skew, and how do you detect it?
  4. What backs the Databricks online feature store, and what are its sync modes?
  5. What status were Feature Views in when checked?

Answers

  1. It uses only values known at or before the prediction time of each row.
  2. A value for a past period may have been published or restated later. Using it would leak future knowledge.
  3. Different feature values in production than in training. Detect it by logging served features and comparing them with offline values for the same keys and times.
  4. Lakebase (autoscaling Postgres). Sync modes are TRIGGERED (the default), CONTINUOUS and SNAPSHOT.
  5. Public Preview.

8. Sources

Checked 2026-10-26 through web search.

  • Databricks feature store: https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/machine-learning/feature-store/
  • Online feature store on Lakebase: https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/oltp/projects/feature-store
